documents.title: Письмо А. И. Бергу (Letter to A. I. Berg)
documents.shortName: Kolmogorov, Letter to A. I. Berg (1961)
documents.dateNote: Undated letter; it says Kolmogorov gave the lecture 'Automata and life' 'in the spring of this year', and the commentary dates the lecture 6 April 1961 and the letter to 1961, before the Tekhnika — molodezhi issues of October and November 1961.

records.statement: Kolmogorov's letter to A. I. Berg (1961) restates theses of his lecture 'Automata and life' as he had formulated them for the magazine Tekhnika — molodezhi: if being alive or able to think is defined purely functionally, for example by counting as thinking a material system with which one can reasonably discuss problems of science or literature, then the artificial creation of living and thinking beings must be recognised as feasible in principle.

time.note: Undated letter; 1961 is the editorial commentary's dating (p. 201), from the lecture of spring 1961 and the journal chronology. Exact day unknown.

attested.note: The wording is read in a 2023 typeset edition; the editorial commentary reports an earlier publication of the letter (Novosibirsk, 2001), not seen. The commentary also says the theses were printed separately before the lecture and opened the collection Vozmozhnoe i nevozmozhnoe v kibernetike; neither was seen.

records.qualification: Conditional on a functional definition of thinking. The fourth thesis says that real successes of cybernetics on this path are much more modest than popular books suggest. The commentary contrasts Berg's statement of 1962 that machines do not think and never will; that statement is relayed by the commentary and is not recorded.

evidence.passage: то придется признать в принципе вполне осуществимым ИСКУССТВЕННОЕ СОЗДАНИЕ живых и мыслящих существ.
evidence.note: English: 'then one will have to recognise as fully feasible in principle the ARTIFICIAL CREATION of living and thinking beings.' The condition precedes it in the same sentence: if being 'alive' or able to 'think' is defined purely functionally.

evidence.passage: Системы из очень большого числа элементов, каждый из которых действует чисто «арифметически», могут приобретать качественно новые свойства.
evidence.note: English: 'Systems of a very large number of elements, each of which acts purely "arithmetically", can acquire qualitatively new properties.' Context: a thesis about modelling life and thought.

crossFamily.result: corrected: date note (1961 is an editorial reconstruction). Classification agreed: thesis 3 articulates, thesis 2 is context.

maintainerDecision.effect: Admitted with the attested date (2023); the 1963 printing of the theses is sought.

omissions.item: Russian cosmism (Fedorov, Tsiolkovsky): searched and not included
omissions.reason: Bounds: web searches in Russian on 2026-11-02 for Fedorov's Filosofiya obshchego dela and for Tsiolkovsky on machines or artificial reason; Tsiolkovsky's 'Неизвестные разумные силы' (1928) retrieved (its PDF text layer is not machine-readable: 373 words extracted from a 587 KB file). No full text of Fedorov's work was located from this environment. Scholarship located by the searches discusses Fedorov's 'regulation of nature' and Tsiolkovsky's intelligent beings of other worlds, not machine or artificial intelligence. No primary text was found that explicitly concerns machine or artificial intelligence; the strand is not included. A reader with the texts could search Fedorov for 'машин' and Tsiolkovsky's collected works for 'автомат' and 'искусственн'.

In copyright (Polish original and the 2013 English translation by Joanna Zylinska, University of Minnesota Press); no legally accessible text from this environment, and no author or publisher excerpt was located. Not included; a library task, not an archive retrieval.

omissions.item: John von Neumann: The Computer and the Brain (1958); 'The General and Logical Theory of Automata' (Hixon Symposium 1948, printed 1951)
omissions.reason: No open copy located (the 1958 book is lending-only); not read. The often-quoted remark that von Neumann could build a machine to do anything one could precisely describe is known from later recollections (relays) and was not used.
